white wall movin fast can i run sideways or uphill??

Run sideways, not uphill. Move sideways out of the snow's path as fast as you can. The slide travels downhill, so sideways gets you clear. Do not run uphill or straight down. If you cannot escape, grab a tree or rock and crouch low. If buried, cover your mouth and nose, and try to keep one hand up. Call 911 when you are safe.

Move sideways out of the snow's path now.
1. Grab the kids and run to the side of the slope, not downhill. Avalanche snow flows down and can bury you.
2. Do not hide behind boulders. The snow can bury or crush you there.
3. Get to high ground or a solid building if you can, away from the slide path.
4. Call 911 when you are safe. If anyone is caught, call 911 right away.

Do not run onto the snow. More snow can slide and bury you too.
1. Call 911 now. Say 'avalanche, person buried' and give your location. Rescue teams are needed fast.
2. If you have an avalanche beacon, switch it to search and follow the signal. A buried person can suffocate in minutes.
3. Mark where the person was last seen, then probe the snow with a pole or ski. Probe before you dig.
4. Dig fast with a shovel, from downhill of the signal. Shout for other people to help.
5. Keep watching the slope above you. If it looks like more snow is moving, get clear.

3. Stay quiet and listen. More whumpfs mean it is still unstable.
4. Do not go back onto that slope today.
5. If anyone is buried, call 911 and start beacon search only if trained.

3. If you hear it coming, drop your pack, grab a tree, and cover your mouth.
4. If anyone is buried, call 911 right away.

3. If you are already on the road and see snow, cracks, or hear rumbling, turn back if safe. Do not stop under steep slopes.
4. Call 911 if you are trapped or in danger now.

Yes—move upwind and away now.
1. Go upwind and uphill, away from the ditch. Vapors can travel and collect in low spots.
2. Keep others and pets back. Do not touch the liquid or let it touch skin.
3. Do not start engines, smoke, or use flames nearby. The spill may be flammable.
4. Call 911 and tell them what you see. Give your address from a safe spot.
5. Do not go back until officials say it is safe. Follow their instructions.

Stay inside and keep windows shut.
1. Close all windows and outside doors. Outside air may carry harmful fumes.
2. Turn off fans, AC, and window units. These can pull smoke inside.
3. Move to an inner room and seal gaps with towels or tape. This slows fumes entering.
4. Call 911 if anyone has trouble breathing or the smoke is getting inside. Do not go outside into the smoke unless officials tell you to leave.

3. Call 911 and say you smell something strange and have asthma. Tell them where you are.
4. Tell a teacher or adult if you can, but do not go toward the smell.
5. If you feel wheezing or short of breath, stay calm and keep away from the smell until help comes.

1. Move away from the area first. The plume may still be there.
2. Take off the child's outer clothes and your own. Put them in a bag, away from people.
3. Wash skin and hair with soap and water. Rinse eyes with plain water if they sting.
4. Do not let the child eat or drink until hands are washed.
5. Call 911 if the child has trouble breathing, coughing, or burning skin.

Get inside and take off contaminated clothes first.
1. Move indoors and close windows/doors. The cloud may still be dangerous outside.
2. Remove clothes that touched the cloud and put them in a bag. Clothes hold the chemical against your skin.
3. Shower with lots of lukewarm water and soap. Washing removes chemical from your skin.
4. Do not scrub hard or use hot water. Hot water and scrubbing can hurt skin and increase absorption.
5. Call 911 if anyone has trouble breathing, eye pain, or feels sick. Say it may be a chemical exposure.
If you were not outside in the cloud, you likely do not need to shower.

1. Roll up windows and set air to recirculate. This keeps fumes out of the car.
2. Move away, upwind and uphill if you can. Burnt-plastic fumes can be toxic.
3. If you are already in the smell, get out of it fast and into fresh air.
4. Call 911 and say there is a truck crash with a strong chemical smell. Life may be at risk.
5. If anyone has trouble breathing, dizziness, or burning eyes, call 911 and get to fresh air now.

Do not drink that water.
1. Stop drinking and don't use it for brushing teeth or making ice. Bleach smell and brown color mean it may be unsafe.
2. Drink only bottled or sealed water if you have it.
3. If you have no bottled water, boil tap water for 1 full minute and let it cool before drinking. Boiling kills germs, but if it smells strongly of chemicals, do not drink it at all.
4. If anyone has vomiting, dizziness, or trouble breathing, call 911.

1. Use bottled water if you have it. It is the safest choice.
2. If no bottled water, boil water for 1 minute, then let it cool. Boiling kills germs.
3. If you cannot boil, use unscented household bleach: 8 drops per gallon, wait 30 minutes. This is a backup only.
4. Check official local notices for a boil-water advisory. Follow them.
5. Do not use hose water for drinking, brushing teeth, or washing food until cleared.

1. Wash dishes with soap and tap water if needed, but that alone does not make them safe. Germs or chemicals can stay on them.
2. Rinse with safe water: bottled water, or water boiled and cooled. This removes germs and residue that can make you sick.
3. Let dishes air-dry fully. A dry surface is safer.
4. If you must use tap water, boil it first and let it cool before rinsing. Boiling kills germs.

2. If you have a private well and it is dry or low, the water may be contaminated. Do not drink it without testing.
3. Use bottled water, or boil water for 1 minute and let it cool before drinking.
4. Call 911 only if someone is sick or in danger.

Do not give creek water to livestock until you know it is safe.
1. Keep your own drinking water separate and safe. Creek water can carry germs and farm chemicals.
2. Check the creek first. Look for algae, dead fish, bad smell, or runoff from fields or roads. If you see any, do not use it.
3. If it looks clear, still treat it before hauling. Ask your county extension office or a vet how to make it safe for your animals.
4. Haul only what you can lift safely, and keep children and pets away from the water and vehicle.
5. If animals are already weak or down, call a vet now. Call 911 if a person is in danger.

Store at least 1 gallon per person per day.
1. For 3 people, store a minimum of 9 gallons for 3 days. More is safer: 2 weeks needs about 42 gallons.
2. Use clean food-grade containers. Label the date. Keep them cool and out of sunlight.
3. If tap water is still on, fill clean containers now. Do not drink stored water that looks, smells, or tastes bad.
4. If you must use questionable water, boil it 1 minute, or use unscented bleach per official directions.
5. Call 911 if anyone is sick or dehydrated.

5. Do not drink alcohol or caffeine. They make you lose water.

Drop, cover, and hold on. Do not run outside while the ground is shaking.
1. Get low now. Falling is the main danger.
2. Cover your head and neck under a sturdy table or desk. If none, sit against an inside wall away from windows and tall furniture.
3. Hold on to your cover until the shaking stops. Running outside during shaking risks falling debris and glass.
4. Stay away from the fallen bookcase and windows.
5. After shaking stops, check for injuries. Call 911 if anyone is hurt or trapped.

3. Do not run outside during shaking. Falling glass and debris cause most injuries.

5. Leave by stairs only if the building is damaged. Do not use elevators.

2. Keep the hurt person still. Moving a hurt neck or back can make it worse.
3. Press hard on any bleeding with a clean cloth.

5. Stay put and wait for help unless staying is dangerous.

Get out if you can do it quietly. If not, hide and stay silent.

2. If you cannot leave, get in a room with a lock. Lock it and put something heavy against the door.
3. Stay low and quiet. Silence your phone but keep it. Do not turn on lights.

2. Do not stop under bridges, trees, signs, or beside tall buildings. These can fall.
3. Keep the kids in the car with seatbelts on until shaking stops.
4. Keep insulin cool and out of direct sun. Heat ruins insulin.
5. After shaking stops, check for injuries and road damage before driving.

Call 911 now. He may have heat stroke, which can kill.
1. Check if he is awake and breathing normally. If not breathing, start CPR and tell 911.
2. If awake, move him to shade or cool room and loosen clothing. Heat builds fast.
3. Put ice packs or cool wet cloths on neck, armpits, and groin. These cool him fastest.
4. Do not give food or drink if he is passed out or confused. He could choke.
5. Keep cooling him until help arrives. Do not leave him alone.

Cool your dog right now and get to air conditioning.
1. Pour cool (not ice-cold) water on the dog's belly, paws, and back, and fan it. Fast cooling saves lives in heat.
2. If your car has working AC and fuel, drive somewhere cool now. A cool car is safer than a hot building.
3. If the car is hot or unreliable, stay and keep cooling the dog with water and airflow near a window or door.
4. Call 911 if the dog is vomiting, collapsing, or confused. That can be heatstroke and is an emergency.

Leave for a cool place now if you can drive safely. Heat can kill a dog fast.
1. Start cooling the dog now: wet its coat with cool (not ice-cold) water and put it in front of a fan. Heavy panting is an early warning.
2. Bring water for both of you. Sip often; don't wait until thirsty.
3. If you have a car with AC and fuel, drive to a cool place (library, mall, cooling center, friend's home).
4. If you can't drive, call 911 for help. Say the dog is panting hard and the power is out.
5. Never leave the dog in a parked car. Call 911 if the dog collapses, vomits, or seems confused.

Call 911 now. Drowsy, hot, and vomiting can be heat stroke, which is life-threatening.
1. Call 911 and say the child may have heat stroke. Do not wait to see if they get better.
2. Move the child to a cool place out of the heat and sun. Start cooling right away.
3. Loosen or remove extra clothing. Cool the skin with cool water and fan air on them.
4. Only if the child is fully awake, give small sips of cool water. Do not give drinks if they are very drowsy or hard to wake.
5. Stay with the child until help comes. Do not leave them alone.

2. Move to the lowest, coolest room. Heat rises.
3. Put wet cloths on your neck, wrists, and head. This cools you.
4. Open windows only if outside air is cooler and safe. Otherwise keep sun out.

1. Check the kids. If anyone is confused, limp, vomiting, or won't wake, call 911 now. Heat stroke is deadly.
2. Cool them fast. Wipe skin with cool wet cloths, fan them, remove extra clothes.
3. Move to the coolest place you can — a shady spot, basement, or a car with AC.
4. Give small sips of water only if they are awake and alert.
5. If your home stays very hot, go somewhere cooler.

Wake your kids and get everyone outside right now. Do not open windows first.
1. Leave the house immediately. A spark can cause an explosion.
2. Do not flip light switches, use phones, or light anything inside. Even a small spark can ignite gas.
3. Take the kids out, then call 911 from outside. Only then report the gas smell.
4. Do not go back inside until firefighters say it is safe.
Opening windows is not safe as a first step. It wastes time and does not remove the danger.

Pull over safely and stop the car now.
1. Turn off the engine and do not restart it. A spark can ignite gas vapor.
2. Get everyone, including your mom, out and walk upwind, away from the car. Gas vapor can catch fire.
3. Do not smoke, use lighters, or use phones near the car until you are well away.
4. Call 911 once you are a safe distance away. A gas smell in a car can mean a leak or fire risk.
5. If anyone feels dizzy, confused, or has a headache, tell 911 — it may be carbon monoxide.

2. Do not stay to reset it or look for the cause. Leave the building.
3. Call 911 from outside. Say the CO alarm is sounding.
4. Do not go back in until firefighters say it is safe. A low-battery chirp and a real alarm can sound alike, so let them check.
